EICMA 2026 • Benelli Showed the World Its New Tornado Naked Tre 903 Concept at EICMA 2026 and It's a Triple!
Subaru's New TY85 Manual-Equipped WRX STI Sport R Clocks Over 1,000 Orders in Less Than Two Days
16 photos
Photo: Subaru
Subaru doesn't need a limited-run special edition of the WRX to convince Japanese enthusiasts that a manual boxer-engined sedan with all-wheel drive is worth buying. Enter the STI Sport R, which attracted 600 orders on its first day on sale. By the following afternoon, it had passed 1,000 orders.
Said numbers come from Japanese motoring publication Creative Trend, which cites a Subaru dealership contact. Per the cited publication, there is a possibility that orders will be suspended on Sunday, November 22nd. The folks at Subaru originally intended a 1,000-unit initial production run, but Creative Trend understands that Subaru has increased it to 1,500 vehicles.
In any case, production figures will be revealed little by little in the following months. Back in October 2026, the company reported a year-to-date global production total of 647,145 units for the period through September 2026, representing an increase of 4.0 percent from the same period last year. Of the grand total, domestic production accounted for 363,770 vehicles.
For a Scooby that isn't a special edition, the WRX STI Sport R's opening salvo is quite impressive. The first-day orders alone amounted to almost twice the planned 330-unit monthly sales estimate for Japan, and this brings us to the WRX STI Sport+. Restricted to only 600 examples, the # was allocated through a lottery. At the time, Subaru recorded more than 9,000 applications for said 600 vehicles.
The attraction is fairly easy to understand. Japanese enthusiasts waited a long time for a regular-production WRX with a manual, and the STI Sport R's transmission is no regular manual. Referred to as TY85 , said heavy-duty manual differs from the TY75 offered in the US-market WRX in many respects, beginning with its higher torque capacity and mechanical rod linkage versus a cable setup.
Photo: Subaru Everyone who loves manuals prefers a more tactile and direct mechanical connection to the gears, right? Subaru's engineers also reworked the shift mechanism, cutting shift play by 60 percent for more precise throws. Developed from the Japanese automaker's Super Taikyu know-how, the auto rev-match feature matches engine speed as intended on downshifts for smoother transitions.
Of course, you can turn off the system to heel-and-toe manually. Last but certainly not least, the TY85 is an ex-WRX STI transmission. Despite its origins, the STI Sport S uses a viscous coupler instead of the DCCD system we all know and love. Under the hood, it's not much of an STI either in regard to peak output.
Its 2.4-liter turbo flat-four mill belts out 202 kilowatts, which should be read as 271 horsepower in the US or 275 in Europe, with Subaru claiming peak power at 5,600 revolutions per minute. 375 Newton-meters (277 pound-feet) can be enjoyed from 2,000 to 4,800 revolutions per minute.
Said numbers aren't nearly enough to frighten Merc's old-gen A 35 with the 2.0-liter turbo I4, let alone the S version of the A 45 and other compacts that received the 45-series treatment.
Beyond its trick manual tranny, the STI Sport R also gets reworked electronic throttle and boost pressure control for improved response across the entire rev range. ZF electronically controlled dampers also need mentioning, plus Brembo six- and two-piston monoblock calipers working with drilled brake discs.
5,480,000 yen is the starting price of the WRX, including the consumption tax. At current exchange rates, the Japan-only model costs just under 34,500 bucks.

Cargo theft losses reached an estimated $304.6 million in the second quarter of 2026, more than double the $135.7 million recorded a year earlier, according to Verisk CargoNet . Reported incidents fell 26% to 677, which means fewer thefts are causing far larger losses.
In a recent FWTV interview at FreightWaves F3, Aqil Naeem, co-founder and CEO of E3 Group , said reported numbers likely miss a meaningful share of what is happening. “We have customers of ours that are losing over $50 million a year in cargo losses, they’re just not reporting it,” Naeem said.
The reason, he explained, is reputational. “When you’re a shipper and you’re losing cargo, that looks bad for your brand,” he said. When he asks E3’s customers whether they share data with CargoNet, “a lot of them just opt out of it.”
That gap matters because the trends inside E3’s customer base look different from the headline statistics. Naeem said he can’t speak to trailer hijackings, but in one category he was unequivocal: “Amongst my customer base, fictitious pickup and deception are 100% on the rise.”
Higher-value targets, higher-value losses
Reported fictitious-pickup incident counts have been roughly flat, moving from 165 to 158 year over year in the data discussed during the interview. The cost per incident, however, has climbed. Naeem attributes that less to inflation than to what criminals are choosing to steal. Thieves, he said, are increasingly passing on low-value cargo in favor of higher-value freight, particularly “data center moves.”
He said he recalls seeing a statistic that roughly 92% of stolen high-tech equipment involves fictitious pickups and deception. The scale of a single loss can be enormous. Journalists have contacted him about $40 million loads of GPUs, which on their own would account for more than 10% of the quarterly total cited above.
When everything checks out, and the wrong person shows up
What makes modern fictitious pickup so hard for brokers and shippers to catch is that the paperwork often holds up. Naeem described a pattern in which criminals rely on a valid carrier’s credentials to get through onboarding, then send someone else to collect the freight.
“Everything checks out,” he said. “There might be someone on the inside who shares a pickup number, and the person who actually comes to the gate is different.”
Naeem reviews the thefts his customers have experienced, and the pattern is consistent. “I haven’t seen a single cargo theft happen with an MC that would have failed a carrier vetting solution,” he said. “The real problem is that people are working with good carriers. But information is leaking.”
That leaked information, he said, has a market. He described black markets where pickup codes for large enterprise shippers are traded. “For $5,000, $10,000, you can go ahead and buy a pickup code, the appointment, and the information you need,” Naeem said. “You buy a magnet, you impersonate a carrier, and there’s nothing stopping you from picking up that freight.”
Business email compromise remains a common entry point for sophisticated schemes, but Naeem framed it as a symptom of a broader exposure rather than the root cause. A breached inbox, he said, gives a criminal visibility into pickup codes and pickup times. In his view, it is “more of a logistics question,” and he would not treat solving breached email as the ultimate fix, even though it is the easiest way for someone to get that information.
Rethinking where verification happens
That diagnosis shapes E3’s product. The company positions itself as a driver verification platform built around confirming that the person arriving at pickup is actually affiliated with the carrier the broker booked.
Naeem argued that carrier vetting has reached its limits as a standalone defense. “Increasingly, carrier vetting is starting to become not only commoditized but ineffective,” he said. “You’re essentially doing LLC verification. The person who comes can be completely different.”
He said that regardless of how much customers have invested in vetting, “they just have not seen cargo thefts decline.” He added that he doesn’t know “a single top 25 brokerage” he has spoken with that has seen thefts decline over the past two years.
E3’s approach unifies information from three parties: the broker, the driver and the shipper. The shipper can then confirm that the driver at the gate was actually sent by that broker. According to Naeem, E3 verifies more than 6,000 drivers per day and has verified over 800,000 loads without a single cargo theft incident.
The driver experience, and the 4% who don’t finish
Any verification step adds friction, and drivers are the ones who feel it. E3 reports a 96% seamless completion rate, and Naeem said driver completion is “arguably the most important factor when it comes to driver verification.”
The remaining 4% is revealing, he said. Common drop-off points include drivers who are masking their IP location and decline to turn off a VPN when asked, and drivers unwilling to provide a picture of their CDL. “Obviously, someone who is fraudulent is not going to try to attempt to get through a verification process,” he said.
E3 frames the product as a tool for drivers rather than a hurdle. “We try to be a driver-centric brand,” Naeem said, adding that he talks about the product on SiriusXM and gets “dozens of emails weekly from drivers thanking us for the product.”
Deterrence through identity
One scenario tests the model: a real, credentialed driver working with a theft ring. Naeem said the verification process itself changes the risk calculation. A driver provides a name, vehicle and VIN information, and potentially ELD connections. “You have essentially created the greatest identity profile that any police or any sort of person trying to combat cargo theft would ever want,” he said.
With that much information on file, including a home address, Naeem said, “you are essentially taking on the biggest gamble of your life if you try to steal a load from one of our customers.” That, he argued, is why some would-be thieves drop out of the process.
Handling sensitive driver data
Collecting selfies and CDL scans raises obvious questions about who sees that data. Naeem said E3’s algorithm processes the information and that customers choose their own level of exposure. Some customers “will not want us to show them the CDL at all,” he said, while others “want us to store it in their Snowflake DB, and they want the custody of that data. We can support both sides of the spectrum.”
He also recommended that brokers avoid keeping CDL information in their own systems. “I know brokers that have 1000s of CDLs that they have never deleted,” he said, describing them as $1,000 fines sitting in inboxes, waiting for someone to claim them.
Guarantees, liability and misdirection
On coverage, Naeem was direct about how E3’s guarantee works. The company refunds its fees if an authenticated load is stolen, but cargo loss itself would fall to insurance. “Cargo loss has not happened yet on our platform. The insurance would hold it,” he said. E3 is working toward covering losses itself, he added, and if a customer experiences a theft, “just text me, and I’ll cover the deductible at that point.”
Another vulnerability is misdirection after the driver leaves the facility. Naeem said E3 addresses it with driver instructions. Drivers receive the shipper’s requirements and are asked to confirm their destination. If a driver enters a different location, as can happen with double-brokered freight, E3 flags a risk incident, escalates it and takes the driver off the load. Drivers are also told that if anyone asks them to change course, they should call the broker’s number, not their dispatcher.
Naeem acknowledged the limits. A driver willing to hand over all of their information and then be misdirected on purpose might still become an incident, he said, though he argued that kind of brazenness is unlikely. “We live in a country with laws,” he said.
A liability question, not just a theft question
Naeem closed with a message for brokers who may never buy E3’s product but should rethink their exposure. Verifying who actually comes to the pickup, he said, is “not only essential for cargo theft, but increasingly liability.”
He pointed to litigation as evidence, citing Hardy v. Singh , in which he said parties were found liable for failing to check whether a carrier was double brokering freight, and a suit he said C.H. Robinson and Unilever currently face. “It’s not just a cargo theft question now; it’s becoming a liability question,” Naeem said.
For shippers and brokers watching losses climb despite stronger carrier vetting, the takeaway from Naeem’s argument is that the control point may need to move. The credentials can be valid and the carrier can be sound. The open question is whether the person at the gate belongs there.

1924 Federal-Knight Truck Sat for 70 Years, Sleeve-Valve Engine Wants To Live
10 photos
Photo: Jennings Motor sports/YouTube
Are you a fan of revival videos, but you've seen one too many Chevrolet Tri-Five features? Well, how about seeing a 1924 Federal truck spring back to life? Haven't heard about Federal up until now? No worries, I love to tell stories about orphan brands.
The Federal Motor Truck Company came to be in 1910, but it was actually born as Bailey. It was headquartered in Detroit, Michigan, operating a factory on Leavitt Street. Federal's main competitor was Diamond T, a far more iconic truck manufacturer.
Perhaps the most interesting bit of info about Federal is that it was founded by Martin L. Pulcher, who was part of the small founding group at Oakland Motor Car Company. The latter was purchased by GM and eventually spawned the Pontiac brand in 1926.
Federal was somewhat successful until the late 1940s, with production reaching as many as 3,500 trucks per year. Peak sales hit 10,000 units in 1947. The company was eventually sold to NAPCO, which was famous for four-wheel drive vehicle parts. NAPCO closed down Federal's Detroit plant and moved all tooling to Minneapolis. The company was shut down in March 1960.
The truck you see here was born in 1924, at a time when Federal was doing quite good. 1924 was actually a banner year for the company, as the city of Detroit had officially renamed Leavitt Street to Federal Street. Moreover, it was the second consecutive year when Federal outsold its primary rival, Diamond T.
1924 also marked the introduction of Federal's light delivery truck, powered by a Willys-Knight sleeve-valve engine. It was marketed as the Federal-Knight and remained in production through 1927. This weathered truck is one of those rigs.
Reportedly parked for a whopping 70 years, this hauler is in pretty bad shape overall. But at the same time, it's also in surprisingly good condition for a vehicle that sat for this long. I mean, it's still in one piece, rust isn't terrible yet, and it's still very much complete. Moreover, it still has the original sleeve-valve four-cylinder engine under the hood.
Patented by Charles Knight in 1904, this engine replaced traditional poppet valves, springs, and camshafts with rotating cylindrical sleeves placed around the pistons. Similar engines were also used by Daimler and Panhard, but the design became obsolete after World War II. Knight's engine is a whopping 100 years old, and seeing one in such condition is absolutely amazing.
And you know what's even more amazing? The fact that our host managed to get it to fire up. It doesn't idle just yet, and this truck is far from being road-worthy, but hey, it's definitely better than rotting away in a junkyard.
Will we see this truck back on the road anytime soon? Well, that's a question I cannot answer, and the owner didn't say a word about it. But it's a great opportunity to see a rare Federal truck that's not a rust bucket .

New John F. Kennedy Aircraft Carrier Launches and Recovers F‑35C Jets for the First Time
8 photos
Photo: Lockheed Martin
Back in the middle of October, an undisclosed patch of water somewhere near the U.S. saw something unique unfolding: for the first time, two Lockheed Martin F‑35C Lightning II fighter jets repeatedly took off and landed on the deck of the newest aircraft carrier in the world. It was, as the parties involved said when they announced the achievement this week, the start of a new chapter in naval aviation.
The PCU John F. Kennedy (CVN 79, soon-to-be USS John F. Kennedy) is by all accounts and purposes, the newest ship of this kind in the world. Part of the new Gerald R. Ford-class, it is currently undergoing final qualification testing, and that includes the launches and recoveries I mentioned above.
That's something any new aircraft carrier needs to do, so they all go through such things, but the tests seem even more important for the Kennedy. That's because it debuts a completely new operating environment, centered around a revised Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS) meant to send aircraft on their way in a more controlled manner, and the Advanced Arresting Gear (AAG) that catches them more effectively.
As if that wasn’t enough, there is also a redesigned flight deck and island at play on this ship, one that changes airflow, exhaust dynamics, and deck operations.
We are told that last month the two F-35s , dispatched from Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland, were at it, testing all of the above for 11 days in a row. During this time, they performed 34 flights, 122 catapult launches, and 122 arrested landings, all of them to perfection.
The tests performed in October went far beyond the Kennedy's ability to launch and recover its planes, as they went deeper into checking software and shipboard installations of the EMALS and AAG, but also the loads and structural models for the launch and recovery of the F-35.
The John F. Kennedy is the second aircraft being developed in the Gerald R. Ford-class – the first one, wearing the name of the class, was commissioned back in 2017 - and it is presently still undergoing sea trials, with its actual entry into service expected sometime next year.
The massive ship can accommodate 4,660 crew and up to 90 combat aircraft. Because it is nuclear-powered, it has the ability to stay at sea indefinitely, as long as it's constantly supplied with food and fuel for the jets. Its pair of nuclear reactors and four shafts push it over the waves at speeds of 35 mph (56 kph).
The Kennedy may be the second carrier of the Ford class, but it won't be the last. Work is ongoing on another four, named Enterprise (CVN 80), Doris Miller (CVN 81, William J. Clinton (CVN 82), and George W. Bush (CVN 83). Another four carries on top of these are yet to be named.

American Samoa is a US territory covering seven South Pacific islands and atolls. ( Stock image of healthy coral reef in American Samoa The Ocean Agency. )
Posted By: Cecilia Jamasmie November 20, 2026
The United States government pressed ahead with its first offshore critical minerals auction on Thursday, drawing US$6 million (C$8.6 million) in winning bids despite local opposition and a court setback earlier in the week.
Deep-sea mining startup Wetstone US Ventures offered the minimum US$3 million for each of two proposed 20-year leases covering about 127,500 sq. km. of seabed off American Samoa . It was the only bidder to submit offers, although another participant had registered. The bids require review before leases can be issued.
“We had hoped it would never come to this,” Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of American Samoan environmental group Finafinau, said in a statement Thursday.
“We are here at Moana Rising because our people deserve more than being heard and ignored. They deserve a meaningful say in decisions that will affect generations. Ocean rights are human rights, and our home is not for sale.”
The auction advances President Donald Trump’s April 2025 directive to accelerate access to critical minerals on the ocean floor and reduce reliance on foreign supplies.
Legal challenges
Three lawsuits have challenged the process, including one that produced Monday’s ruling.
Judge Jill A. Otake of the federal district court in Hawaii on Nov. 16 invalidated a National Marine Fisheries Service consultation that had failed to consider the full effects of exploration and mining on protected marine life. Her order did not expressly bar the auction.
The Marine Minerals Administration told the Associated Press it had begun renewed consultations with the fisheries service after the ruling, but declined to postpone the auction.
The sale took place at the Ventura County Fire Department headquarters in Thousand Oaks, Calif., where several dozen protesters gathered outside.
2024 moratorium
American Samoa imposed a moratorium on deep-sea mining in its territorial waters in 2024. The auction areas lie in federal waters beyond that jurisdiction. Territorial leaders and village councils also opposed federal leasing plans, while most of the more than 76,000 public comments submitted to the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management objected to offshore mining.
In a lawsuit filed Oct. 19, a council of Samoan chiefs, known as matai, and community groups represented by Earthjustice challenged the federal government’s authority to lease seabed areas off the territory.
The plaintiffs argue that the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act does not authorize mineral leasing off U.S. territories and that the sale violates historic treaty requirements concerning American Samoa.
A separate lawsuit filed Nov. 18 by Finafinau and the Natural Resources Defense Council seeks to invalidate any leases issued through the auction.
“We will use the full extent of the law to vigorously push for the leases to be voided,” Earthjustice attorney Chris Eaton said in a statement.
Earthjustice also represented Fa’asao Amerika Samoa and the Conservation Council of Hawaii in the Endangered Species Act lawsuit filed Aug. 18 that led to Monday’s ruling.
Next steps
If issued, the leases would permit limited preliminary activities and give Wetstone exclusive rights to submit exploration, testing and mining plans. They would not authorize mineral delineation, testing or mining, which require further approvals.
Commercial deep-sea mining remains at an experimental stage. The sale targets metals found in polymetallic nodules and ferromanganese crusts on the seafloor.
The Trump administration is also considering seabed lease auctions near the Northern Mariana Islands, Virginia and Alaska. Separately, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is reviewing applications under U.S. law for mining in areas beyond national jurisdiction. Print

If it came to fruition, the rumored deal between Sanofi and Insmed would likely be the year’s largest, with one analyst putting a potential value for the biotech as high as $40 billion.
Insmed shares popped more than 20% on Thursday amid rumors of a potential Sanofi buyout that some analysts are estimating could be valued around $40 billion.
Sanofi is “weighing an acquisition,” Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter.
BMO Capital Markets called the potential deal a “clear strategic fit,” writing in a Thursday note that it would add “Insmed’s differentiated respiratory growth engine to Sanofi’s existing commercial infrastructure in the therapeutics category.”
“A Sanofi/Insmed deal could potentially represent the largest transaction of the year,” the analysts noted, though they said that “discussions likely remain ongoing, and other potential bidders could emerge.” Neither company commented to Bloomberg on a potential transaction.
Insmed closed trading on Thursday at $144 per share, up from its closing price of $120 apiece the previous day. The current value of $144 multiplied by around 219 million shares puts a potential deal at close to $31.5 billion , while Bloomberg placed Insmed at a valuation of around $26.6 billion.
William Blair analysts agreed with the potential fit, saying on Thursday that a deal between the companies “particularly makes sense in light of the commercial push into COPD with the recent Dupixent approval.”
The blockbuster biologic—which Sanofi shares with long-time partner Regeneron— was approved to treat chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in September 2024.

Regeneron and Sanofi’s Dupixent Tipped to Dominate COPD Biologics Market
Analysts expect the partners’ first-mover advantage, clinical data and existing presence in lung disease to translate into significant sales, with GlobalData predicting Dupixent’s COPD revenues will top $6.5 billion within 10 years.

Insmed, meanwhile, markets Brinsupri, which was approved in August 2025 for patients 12 years and older with non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis (NCFB). The DPP1 inhibitor was the first treatment for bronchiectasis—a chronic pulmonary disorder—to reach the U.S. market. The company’s other marketed product is Arikayce, an antibiotic approved for hard-to-treat mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) lung disease.
Guggenheim in a Thursday note estimated peak sales for the two products—plus late-stage candidate treprostinil palmitil inhalation powder (TPIP)—at around $15 billion. TPIP is in Phase 3 development for pulmonary hypertension associated with interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and Phase 2 for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
William Blair said a deal between Insmed and Sanofi would make strategic sense—if the latter has the capacity. “[A] big question is whether Sanofi can truly afford an acquisition in the $40 billion range with current net debt of about €12 billion [$13.2 billion,” the analysts said.
However, there are ways such a feat could be accomplished. “Some investors have speculated whether the Insmed assets could be added to Sanofi’s joint venture with Regeneron . . . to provide additional capital to reach necessary valuations,” the firm noted. Sanofi paid Regeneron $1 billion upfront in early October to continue the search for a successor for Dupixent, which loses patent protection in 2031.
If it does happen, an acquisition of this size would be a statement for new CEO Belén Garijo, who took the reins in April after former CEO Paul Hudson was let go in February. But it would fit right in with comments Garijo made on the French pharma’s third quarter call last month.
Sanofi plans to use its “robust cash flow generation to fund business development and M&A transactions, in particular with a focus on later-stage and/or commercial opportunities,” the CEO said.
Sanofi CFO François Roger added on the call that a “strong balance sheet and low leverage allow us to access external financing” to fund deals for the next set of growth drivers.

For much of the past few years, industrial tenants had the luxury of time. Options were plentiful, negotiations dragged and “let’s see what else is out there” was a viable strategy. That window is narrowing.
In a recent market update conversation with Thomas Wasson, Brandon Page , executive vice president and head of leasing and customer solutions at Link Logistics , described a market where demand is building, competition for space is returning and the criteria that decide a lease are shifting. Link Logistics is one of the largest owners and operators of last-mile industrial real estate in North America, with nearly 500 million square feet across the U.S. and Canada. Page oversees portfolio leasing strategy and works closely with its largest customers, which gives him a front-row view of what occupiers want.
For carriers, 3PLs, shippers and anyone else whose network depends on where buildings sit and how they perform, his read is worth a close look.
Demand Is Broadening
Page said demand has built steadily for months. “I would say demand has consistently accelerated throughout the year,” he said, adding that the momentum began toward the end of last year and has continued.
He sorted the drivers into tiers. The most dominant is the AI data center ecosystem, which generates activity during construction and again during ongoing maintenance, alongside advanced manufacturing and reshoring investments that are starting to come online. “We want to own the buildings that are adjacent to [the data centers] to help support those facilities,”Page said.
The second tier is the bread-and-butter freight demand: e-commerce and omnichannel distribution, which follows the consumer and the push toward same-day and next-day delivery. Third-party logistics providers, historically Link Logistics’ largest occupiers, continue to move steadily. Page also pointed to cold storage and to defense and aerospace as specialty segments with new momentum, citing a recently announced Anduril investment likely to affect markets such as Baltimore.
Fast Movers Win
Even as demand builds, Page said tenant decision-making is still deliberate. Customers and their brokers take time to understand a facility and all of its costs. But the dynamics are changing. “We are starting to see situations where we have multiple customers and prospects going after the same building,” he said, noting it’s something Link Logistics saw regularly during COVID.
The implication for occupiers is clear. “Those that are moving quicker are having better success than those that are sort of paralysis by analysis,” Page said.
That message extends to the brokers who represent those tenants. The market remains fairly balanced, he said, but there are more tailwinds than headwinds for landlords heading into year-end than a year ago. Brokers need to prepare clients for rents that will change as markets tighten. “The days of having five or 10 options in a market are gone, and they may have one or two,” he said.
Data Centers Move From Footnote to Force
A couple of years ago, data center-related leasing was a very small part of Link Logistics’ activity. Now it’s a meaningful share. “15% of Link’s new leasing activity over the past year is tied to data centers,” Page said.
He offered a rule of thumb for the scale of the spillover. “Each gigawatt of data center capacity generates roughly 2 million feet,” he said. “We actually think in some cases it’s closer to 2.5 million feet of associated demand.”
Just as important for landlords is how long that demand lasts. Page said 80% of data center-driven demand is long term, with tenants that help stand up facilities and then stay on for ongoing maintenance. The other 20% sign two- to three-year leases focused on setup. “Which is a good tailwind as well for industrial,” he said.
Balancing Scale and Proximity
Two trends in building size can look contradictory but reflect the same goal of efficiency. For large users, Page described “a clear trend of consolidating those 200,000 to 400,000 square foot buildings,” sometimes folding two or three of them into a single facility of about 1 million square feet. Running three buildings means three sets of capital investment and management teams, he said, “just three times the work.” Class A buildings, with their cubic efficiency, tend to lease first.
For last-mile and omnichannel users, the equation flips toward proximity. Link Logistics’ portfolio is largely multi-tenant infill space close to customers, and in those cases, Page said, location can matter more than state-of-the-art specs. “You can’t beat location and access,” he said. Big retail customers are working to get as close to consumers as possible, sometimes delivering in as little as 30 minutes. Whether an order ships from a store or a warehouse, he said, the answer is increasingly “all the above.”
3PLs play a particular role in this environment. Page called them “the fastest way to stand up or modify your national supply chain network,” with less capital tied up than a company standing up its own facility. Large national 3PLs can reposition their portfolios as client needs change.
The New First Question: How Much Power?
If one shift stood out from Link Logistics’ customer advisory council, a roughly 15-member group of the heads of real estate at some of its largest occupiers, it was power. Page said the traditional priority list once ran labor, transportation costs, then rent. Today, “clearly power is the number one driver.”
The numbers show why. A 400,000-square-foot building once came with a 2,000-amp panel. “The new baseline is roughly 4,000 amps,” Page said. Tenants may not use it all on day one, but they’re planning for fleet electrification, extensive material handling and robotics.
The key, he said, is that tenants don’t necessarily need the power immediately. “They don’t necessarily need to have power today, but they need to have a path to power.” They want to know how much capacity is possible and how long it will take to get there, whether six, 12 or 18 months, so they can use other facilities in their network to compensate in the meantime.
Page said some searches now open with the question before any other building attribute is discussed. “‘How much power does it have?’ is line item one,” he said. Square footage and location follow.
Automation: Talked About More Than Deployed
For all the attention on warehouse robotics, Page offered a reality check. “Less than 5% of our facilities actually have automation in there,” he said. Only a handful of Fortune 100 companies can afford the infrastructure and also have the volume to justify it. Costs are falling and systems are becoming more modular, but “it’s still very cost prohibitive for many customers at this point.”
Perception of utilization varies, too. One customer may call a 40-foot-clear building full when product is floor-stacked, while another operating multiple levels of material handling may call itself 90% utilized. It depends, Page said, on the business, the throughput and the technology investment.
Deal Flags: Credit, Term and Flexibility
Asked about red and green flags in closing a deal, Page started with a short rule. “Credit’s king,” he said. A building’s value is tied to the underlying credit and the quality of the rent stream, and short terms on a building that takes significant time to stand up are another warning sign. On the positive side, he points to good-credit tenants investing real capital in a facility, which signals it’s a key part of their network and likely to stay.
For tenants, especially smaller companies where rent is a bigger share of total cost, Page cautioned against focusing only on the face rate. They should ask what capital improvements may be needed and whether the owner can accommodate change. An owner with 50 buildings in a market can offer more room to grow or relocate than one with a single facility. “Make sure you’re partnering with somebody that’s flexible,” he said.
The growth of smaller e-commerce brands and shifts such as the Amazon–UPS breakup on small parcels may also create openings for local and regional 3PLs, Page said.
What to Watch Next
Looking out six to 12 months, Page flagged two open questions. The first is data centers: the election outcome may change sentiment in certain markets, and it remains to be seen how investment from large data center companies plays out. The second is the consumer. Warehouse occupiers aren’t as exposed to interest rates as homebuyers are, he noted, so employment and the underlying health of the economy matter most. When people are employed, they buy more, and Link Logistics’ customers take more space to deliver it efficiently.
That dynamic, Page said, becomes a flywheel as one retailer’s gains force others to follow, “a race to speed,” in his words, that means “you just have to be in a lot more locations and as close to the customers you possibly can get.”
For freight and logistics leaders, the takeaway is practical. Evaluate sites earlier, ask about power first and be ready to decide faster, because the other tenant may already be touring the building.

Pacific Fusion said the New Mexico Environment Department (NMED) has approved the company’s radioactive materials license. The move announced November 20 will enable Pacific Fusion to operate a fusion machine and supports the group’s efforts to commercialize fusion energy in the state.
The license authorizes Pacific Fusion to possess and use tritium fuel for fusion at the company’s $1-billion Research and Manufacturing Campus in Albuquerque. The move marks the first time state officials have issued a radioactive materials license to a private fusion company.
The license approval will keep Pacific Fusion on track toward its goal of net facility gain by 2030, which is when a fusion system generates more energy than what is needed to power the fusion reaction. Pacific Fusion on Friday said the company will continue working closely with NMED as construction progresses.
Collaboration With State Officials
The license approval comes a year after Pacific Fusion announced its decision to build a system in New Mexico. The company said it “reflects close collaboration between the company and state officials to advance a first-of-a-kind energy and advanced manufacturing project while maintaining rigorous safety and environmental standards.”
“Leaders across the state have demonstrated what’s possible when government and industry work hand in hand to deploy new energy technologies,” said Carrie von Muench, co-founder and COO of Pacific Fusion. “This license is an essential milestone on our path to putting clean fusion energy on the grid, and we’re grateful to the New Mexico Environment Department for their commitment to helping us move quickly and responsibly. We’re proud to be building the future of fusion energy here in New Mexico.”
“New Mexico is proving that we can lead the clean energy transition while creating good-paying jobs and building the industries of the future,” said New Mexico Environment Secretary James Kenney. “Our Energy Transition Act set ambitious goals for a zero-carbon electricity future, and innovations like fusion could play an important role in helping us achieve them. Today’s milestone is another clear step forward, demonstrating that New Mexico has the talent, infrastructure and commitment to lead the next generation of clean energy innovation while ensuring protections for public health and the environment.”
Environmental Regulation
Fusion is regulated in New Mexico by the state’s Environment Department, under a framework similar to that used for hospitals and research facilities. The small amounts of tritium needed by Pacific Fusion will be contained in a closed system. Any waste will be disposed of at a licensed facility outside the state in a safe manner, according to the company.
Pacific Fusion’s Research and Manufacturing Campus is expected to create more than 200 permanent jobs, along with hundreds of construction jobs. The company said it has expanded its manufacturing operations in Los Lunas, and to-date has hired 90 workers at its Los Lunas Build Center to build the modular components that will power its pulser fusion system.
“New Mexico has the opportunity to become a national center for America’s fusion energy ecosystem,” von Muench said. “The state’s leadership, scientific expertise and commitment to advanced manufacturing make it an ideal place to build. We’re excited about what this milestone means, not just for Pacific Fusion, but for the jobs, investment and long-term economic opportunity that fusion can bring to New Mexico.”
— Darrell Proctor is a senior editor for POWER.

Alloying Error Prompts 2022 to 2026 Toyota Tundra Exhaust Camshaft Recall
32 photos
Photo: Toyota / edited
Toyota's half-ton pickup faces a new recall, and the problem with the subject population boils down to a manufacturing mistake that should have never made it past quality control. Toyota claims the camshaft supplier added alloy additives twice during the production of a 400-piece batch, pushing magnesium content way beyond Toyota's specifications.
Magnesium is a strong carbide stabilizer, forcing the formation of brittle intercellular iron carbides. Subsequent machining created small cracks in those 400 exhaust-side cams, and those cracks are certain to grow in time until they break. Such a failure would automatically result in a loss of motive power, increasing the risk of a crash.
Toyota initially estimated approximately 300 potentially affected cams. The media release published by the world's largest automaker is pretty lacking in terms of details, but on the other hand, the Part 573 safety recall report published by the NHTSA answers most curiosities. For example, 13502-F4010 is the part number of the subject bank one exhaust camshaft.
CWC Textron is listed as the supplier, and the recall population is split between 2022 - 2023 and 2025 - 2026 models. Unfortunately, the Part 573 report fails to explain why 2024 models are not included. In the United States market, no fewer than 62,490 Tundras are being recalled. Hybrids need not apply.
Given that only 400 cams have been produced incorrectly, it goes without saying that fewer than 1 percent of the vehicle population features iffy exhaust cams. The 2025 - 2026 trucks could have received suspect components during production, while older Tundras could have received them as part of a service replacement.
Photo: Toyota The population splits between 17,762 older trucks and 44,728 newer vehicles. In principle, an exhaust cam isn't a terribly complicated piece of kit. Cams rotate in sync with the crankshaft of the twin-turbo V6 engine, and exhaust cams are designed to operate the exhaust valves. Basically, these parts control when spent gases leave the combustion chambers.
Thousands of revolutions per minute is tough on those cams, and that's why the alloy has to be perfectly so for each application. Cracking under repeated mechanical loads is a big no-no. When that happens, a bunch of warning lights may illuminate. Under the hood, the engine may run rougher than normal, misfire, or stall without warning.
The first warning came in October 2025, when Toyota Motor North America received a report alleging a no-start condition and an illuminated warning light. Technicians recovered the engine, tore it apart, and found that its right-hand exhaust cam had snapped. A second report arrived in December of last year, with TMNA finding surface cracks and another broken cam.
Material analysis provided the first useful clue, prompting Toyota Motor North America to contact the supplier. CWC Textron determined that an operator manually added the alloy additives a second time, apparently unaware that the automated system had already accounted for them. The mistake occurred during a shutdown of a casting line due to equipment issues.
All tested components exceeded the internal magnesium limits. By October 30, 2026, Toyota Motor North America had counted 60 warranty claims and 31 field technical reports in the United States of America. Affected owners will be notified by the Japanese automaker between December 28, 2026, and January 11, 2027.

By: Northern Miner Staff November 20, 2026
Traders have booked an estimated 30,000 to 100,000 tonnes of refined copper to ship from the West Coast of the United States to China, reversing a trade that filled American warehouses ahead of a possible U.S. import tariff, BMO Capital Markets said Friday.
China’s Yangshan warrant premium , a benchmark for imported copper held in bonded warehouses, reached a record $500 (C$715.9) per tonne above London prices Thursday. Rising Chinese premiums and a narrowing gap between U.S. and London futures prices have made China a more profitable destination for some traders, BMO analysts Helen Amos and George Heppel wrote from Asia Copper Week in Shanghai.
“Copper units are now starting to leave the U.S. west coast destined for China, an event we had assigned a very low probability to,” Amos and Heppel noted.
BMO identifies the booked cargoes as copper held outside exchange warehouses on the West Coast. It estimates a voyage of about two weeks before the metal reaches China.
Tariff split
The split in the copper market runs deeper than the cost of shipping. Traders BMO spoke to in China generally expect U.S. President Donald Trump to abandon the proposed refined-copper duty. Western market participants still lean towards a tariff, the analysts said.
A July 2025 proclamation by the White House imposed tariffs on semi-finished copper products and derivatives. It also called for further review before a decision on refined-metal duties of 15% from Jan. 1, 2027, and 30% from Jan. 1, 2028.
Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange traded at $12,310.50 per tonne at 5:30 a.m. Toronto time Friday, about 8.2% lower on the week, according to Reuters . The metal had already fallen below $13,000 on Wednesday. BMO linked the sell-off to investors retreating from artificial-intelligence trades, even as physical supplies in China remained tight.
State-owned Chilean producer Codelco, meanwhile, has offered Asian buyers annual contract premiums of $250 to $280 per tonne for 2027, compared with $350 for Chinese buyers this year, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the discussions. China imported just over 140,000 tonnes of Chilean cathode in the first nine months of 2026, down 38% from a year earlier, the report added.
A signal from Washington could arrest the slide. Otherwise, copper may have to fall far enough to curb scrap supply or higher-cost production from leaching, potentially to around $10,000 to $11,000 per tonne, Amos and Heppel said. BMO’s medium-term bullish view on copper is unchanged.

Mexico has introduced new requirements for commercial trucking companies seeking voluntary federal certification.
The new program places greater emphasis on digital monitoring, vehicle weight compliance and internal operational controls as the country works to strengthen highway safety and regulatory oversight .
The Ministry of Infrastructure, Communications and Transportation (SICT) published the new requirements Thursday, Nov. 19, in Mexico’s Official Gazette of the Federation . The notice took effect Friday, Nov. 20.
The framework establishes procedures for trucking companies to obtain approval under a self-regulation program known as Autorregulación (Permisionario Responsable con el Cumplimiento de la Norma) , or Responsible Permittee for Compliance with the Standard.
The program operates under Mexico’s NOM-012-SCT-2-2017 regulation, which governs maximum vehicle weights and dimensions on federally regulated highways.
Although participation is voluntary, companies seeking certification must demonstrate that they have implemented internal systems capable of ensuring compliance with federal transportation requirements.
The initiative represents a shift toward recognizing carriers that can document their own compliance practices rather than relying exclusively on government inspections.
According to the SICT, the objective is to improve highway safety , reduce operational risks and make vehicle inspection and verification procedures more efficient.
The program applies to federally permitted general freight carriers and private freight transportation operations.
Digital monitoring becomes central to compliance
One of the program’s most significant elements is the emphasis on electronic documentation and internal monitoring systems.
According to an executive guide issued by Mexico’s National Association of Private Transport (ANTP), participating companies must maintain a permanent digital system capable of recording shipment information in real time and making those records available to federal transportation authorities.
Carriers can qualify through two principal compliance mechanisms: using their own weighing equipment to verify cargo weights or implementing standardized loading procedures that consistently meet federal weight and dimension limits.
Companies may also combine both approaches.
The requirements place greater responsibility on carriers to verify that trucks meet applicable limits before entering federal highways.
For larger trucking fleets, this could mean integrating weighing systems, dispatch operations, shipment documentation and compliance reporting into existing fleet management platforms.
For smaller carriers, however, adopting and maintaining the necessary technology and administrative processes could create additional expenses.
The SICT notice also authorizes federal authorities to recognize weighing results generated by carriers’ own scales or by operators demonstrating consistent loading procedures.
How trucking companies can obtain certification
The SICT’s General Directorate of Federal Motor Transport (DGAF) will oversee the approval process through its Executive Directorate of Supervision.
According to the ANTP’s guidance, applicants must complete a five-stage process involving documentation, regulatory review and verification.
Companies must first assemble the required application documents and submit them to the DGAF. The agency then reviews the documentation and conducts an inspection visit before the applicant presents the required guarantee and receives final approval.
Approved carriers will receive official identification for participating vehicles.
The ANTP said certification and the corresponding vehicle identification will remain valid for three years, subject to continued compliance.
Vehicles participating in the program must display their license plate numbers in the prescribed manner and carry an official certification identifier.
Carriers must also maintain updated information concerning their vehicles, operating permits, business addresses and changes to their loading or compliance procedures.
The program’s requirements and application procedures are available through the DGAF’s official self-regulation portal .
Random inspections and penalties remain in place
Despite the program’s emphasis on voluntary compliance, Mexican authorities will retain the ability to inspect participating trucks.
The SICT said inspections may be conducted at fixed weight and dimension verification centers or through electronic monitoring devices deployed by federal authorities.
Carriers that violate applicable weight, dimension or safety requirements remain subject to penalties under Mexico’s federal transportation laws.
According to the ANTP, exceeding weight or dimension limits more than three times within a year, measured from the first violation, can result in revocation of certification.
Other violations of the program’s operating guidelines may also lead to revocation.
What the changes mean for Mexico’s trucking industry
The new framework could have significant implications for Mexico’s commercial trucking industry, particularly as carriers face growing pressure to improve safety, operating efficiency and supply chain visibility.
Companies with established fleet management technology, weighing infrastructure and compliance departments may be better positioned to obtain certification.
Those operators could benefit from greater predictability in vehicle verification processes and potentially fewer administrative delays associated with demonstrating compliance.
Smaller carriers and independent operators, meanwhile, may face greater challenges meeting the program’s digital documentation and procedural requirements.
The framework could also encourage greater investment in fleet management software, electronic shipment records, weighing technology and standardized loading systems.
For shippers, the certification program could provide an additional way to evaluate carriers’ operational controls and commitment to regulatory compliance.
The initiative also comes as Mexico’s trucking industry faces broader challenges involving highway security, operating costs and government enforcement.
Why it matters: Mexico’s transportation ministry’s expanded trucking compliance framework program could accelerate the adoption of digital compliance systems across the country’s trucking industry while creating new operational and administrative demands for carriers.

The new data could help boost Revolution Medicines beyond the currently estimated $14.5 billion in peak sales for the recently approved RAS(ON) inhibitor, Truist Securities predicts.
Revolution Medicines has further entrenched Rasonque as the new standard in pancreatic cancer, with early-stage data that exceeded analyst expectations, showing improved response rates and survival in patients with first-line disease.
Rasonque, approved in August for second-line or later treatment of metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma, led to a 60.7% objective response rate (ORR), with complete responses in 8.2% of patients in the first-line setting in combination with two types of chemotherapy. With a median follow-up of 18.3 months, duration response was 11.1 months and progression free survival (PFS) was 12.8 months—exceeding Truist Securities’ expectation of around 10 months. On overall survival, 76.6% of patients reached the 12-month mark; Truist noted that chemotherapy has historically achieved between 8.5 and 11 months.
Tolerability “continues to look manageable,” Leerink Partners wrote on Friday morning. Common adverse events were diarrhea, fatigue and cytopenias.
The results come from 61 patients in the ongoing Phase 1/2 RMC-GI-102 open-label trial and were presented Thursday at the EORTC-NCI-AACR, or triple meeting, in Spain.
“We believe the data further strengthen RVMD’s competitive moat ahead of the ERAS-0015 update and potential competitive readthrough,” Truist Securities wrote on Thursday evening, pointing to a readout from the Phase 1 AURORAS-1 trial expected from rival Erasca on Friday.
The results could boost future sales for Rasonque, which Truist currently has at $14.5 billion at peak. An approval for this first-line indication could come in 2028, according to Truist.

At the American Association for Cancer Research meeting earlier this year, RevMed revealed initial data from this study in just 40 patients. At that time, confirmed ORR was 58%, with 2.5% of patients achieving complete responses. Now, ORR ticked up, complete responses more than tripled and PFS has roughly doubled. This week’s update “builds meaningfully” on that previous result, Truist said.
“We believe this profile sets a high efficacy bar for 1L PDAC and positions Rasonque + GnP [chemotherapy] to potentially become the first approved RASi combination in this setting through RASolute 303, which we currently expect to read out around 2028,” the analyst wrote.
RASolute 303 is a Phase 3 trial of Rasonque alone and in combination with chemo in patients with first line, previously untreated metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
In the meantime, investors will turn their attention to Erasca, a company that RevMed has filed patent litigation against over that company’s pan-RAS molecular glue ERAS-0015. Investors will be looking for clarity on the depth of response in patients with KRAS G12D pancreatic cancer in particular. The trial more broadly features patients with RAS-mutant solid tumors.
Truist expects an ORR of about 40-50% from Erasca’s medicine, with rates as high as 50% or more for the G12D pancreatic cancer population. In these patients, Rasonque alone has achieved a 24% ORR —less than the 33% ORR the drug achieved across all KRAS mutations in the Phase 3 RASolute 302 trial that supported the approval.
Still, Truist wants more data. “We believe ORR alone is unlikely to resolve the competitive debate. Rasonque has already demonstrated statistically significant OS benefit across RAS subtypes in a randomized Phase 3 study,” the analysts wrote. The therapy is also becoming standard in second line PDAC. “In our view, ERAS-0015 and other competitors would ultimately need durable survival data and likely a head-to-head study against Rasonque to fully establish clinically meaningful superiority.”
Truist expects Rasonque to bring in $287 million in the fourth quarter, going on to $1.27 billion for full year 2027—after the therapy booked $198 million in sales for its first quarter on the market.

A California trucking company owner received 30 months in federal prison for participating in a $7.2 million cargo theft scheme. Criminals used legitimate transportation contracts to obtain shipments before diverting merchandise from warehouses across Southern California. The operation involved purchased trucking companies, stolen electronics and fraudulent driver identities. Federal investigators traced the activity from September 2021 through March 2025.
The Justice Department announced the sentence Tuesday, Nov. 17. U.S. District Judge Kenly Kiya Kato ordered Paramvir Singh, 30, to pay $2,210,055 in restitution. Singh pleaded guilty Aug. 13 to conspiracy to commit theft from interstate or foreign shipments. Prosecutors attributed approximately $7,210,056 in stolen merchandise to his criminal conduct. The restitution order is approximately $5 million lower than the attributed losses. Singh’s plea agreement reserved prosecutors’ right to appeal a restitution award below $7.2 million. The available court filings do not explain the discrepancy.
Court records describe how participants secured freight through brokers and online load boards . Drivers arrived at warehouses with tractors, trailers and paperwork identifying their assigned carriers. After collecting merchandise, conspirators either withheld portions of shipments or diverted entire loads. The operation targeted facilities in Walnut, Fontana, Moreno Valley and Chino, California.
On June 23, 2023, Singh and two co-conspirators transported a trailer containing $5 million in stolen cargo. Federal court records identify a truck yard in San Bernardino, California, as the destination. Investigators also uncovered unauthorized identity use during transportation-related activities. A September 2025 indictment detailed the methods behind the multiyear conspiracy.
Trucking companies provided access to freight
Singh owned Janjua Transport, which prosecutors connected to several stolen shipments. Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration records identify the company under USDOT 3620976 and MC 1236841. The Bakersfield, California, carrier listed one truck and one driver. Regulators granted its operating authority June 11, 2021, before revoking it June 14, 2022. The case illustrates how criminals can exploit legitimate carrier authorities to secure freight before diverting shipments.
Federal court filings identify AP Freight Truckline among businesses associated with Singh’s activities. A carrier profile for AP Freight Trucklines Inc. identifies Paramvir Singh as an officer. The court filings use a slightly different company name. The carrier’s registration lists USDOT 3932312 and MC 1457821. Carrier intelligence platform FreightCheck identified shared contact information between the companies. Both listed the same Bakersfield address and email address. Each carrier also reported one truck and one driver. Regulators granted AP Freight Trucklines operating authority Sept. 19, 2022, before revoking it Dec. 27, 2022.
FMCSA records show regulators reinstated AP Freight Trucklines’ authority Feb. 28, 2023. They revoked it again July 26, 2023. Neither company currently holds active interstate operating authority or maintains primary liability insurance on file. According to the government’s sentencing memorandum, Singh reported annual earnings of $4.1 million from Janjua Transport. He also reported $1.5 million annually from the business identified as AP Freight Truckline in court filings. Prosecutors referenced those figures while examining his financial circumstances.
On March 12, 2022, Mandeep Singh, Sandeep Singh and Gurnaik Singh Chauhan collected merchandise from a Fontana warehouse. The indictment identifies all three as purporting to work for Janjua Transport. Paramvir Singh joined them in transferring the shipment into separate vehicles at a nearby storage facility. Prosecutors valued the stolen cargo at $185,734.40.
Additional incidents occurred in Moreno Valley during September and October 2022. Destinations included three California cities: Lebec, Riverside and Rialto. Another shipment was headed to St. George, Utah. None reached their intended delivery locations, according to investigators. Individual losses ranged from approximately $129,000 to more than $421,000.
The operation also involved purchasing established motor carriers . On Sept. 29, 2023, Singh acquired Obey Eagle Inc. and an associated tractor. Court records document Zelle payments between conspirators and the previous owner. Investigators later connected that vehicle to an unsuccessful freight pickup attempt in Mira Loma, California.
Federal filings describe another incident involving a transportation marketplace account. On March 24, 2025, Singh attempted to register with Flexport using another individual’s identification. The indictment identifies Convoy as the company’s associated load board. Prosecutors included the attempted registration among the conspiracy’s final documented activities.
Four defendants await trial
The original indictment named seven defendants. Charges included wire fraud, interstate cargo theft, identity theft and money laundering. Singh’s guilty plea resolved his conspiracy charge involving stolen commercial shipments. Federal prosecutors identified four additional individuals awaiting trial in March 2027. Their charges remain pending, and the defendants retain the presumption of innocence.
Those defendants include Sandeep Singh, 32, of San Bernardino, and Gurnaik Singh Chauhan, 41, of Fontana. Ranjodh Singh, 39, of Bakersfield, also faces trial alongside Elgar Rolando Hernández, 28, of Fontana. The original filing additionally named Mandeep Singh and Harpreet Singh. Tuesday’s announcement did not provide their current case dispositions.
The FBI’s Inland Violent Crime Suppression Task Force investigated the conspiracy. IRS Criminal Investigation and the California Highway Patrol’s Cargo Theft Interdiction Program also participated. Sheriff’s departments in San Bernardino and Riverside counties contributed additional resources. Police agencies in Fontana and San Bernardino also assisted. Federal prosecutors continue pursuing the remaining defendants through the Central District of California.
Why it matters
Criminals exploited legitimate freight transactions to steal millions in cargo without traditional hijackings. Their ability to secure loads and redirect shipments demonstrates how easily fraud can enter routine transportation operations. The case highlights the financial exposure brokers, carriers and shippers face when criminals manipulate established freight processes.
CFCO
The Certified Fraud Compliance Officer (CFCO) program addresses the risks criminals exploit when obtaining freight through legitimate transportation channels. The training emphasizes identifying suspicious booking activity, verifying pickup authorization and recognizing discrepancies before cargo changes hands. A legitimate carrier profile does not eliminate fraud risk when criminals manipulate the people and processes behind a shipment.

Savara shares dropped 18% on the news, though analysts remain confident in approval, instead pointing to potential “bandwidth issues” at the FDA.
The FDA will miss its expected Nov. 22 decision date for Savara’s rare lung disease candidate, with the agency failing to give the biotech a new review deadline.
Savara said on Friday that the FDA had communicated it would not meet its already-delayed PDUFA date. In April, the agency extended the biologics license application review by three months, deeming Savara’s responses to agency information requests as a major amendment to the application.
The now twice-delayed decision centers on Savara’s lead program, called molgramostim or potentially Molbreevi, in autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP), a rare lung condition that can lead to serious complications such as lung fibrosis. If given the greenlight, the inhaled therapeutic would become the first FDA-approved treatment for the condition.
Savara’s stock slid 18% at market open on Friday, dropping to $4.26 per share.
“We expect some stock volatility, as the agency has not assigned a revised PDUFA, nor do we have color as to why the FDA needs additional time to review,” Jefferies analysts wrote Friday.
However, because the FDA postponed its decision rather than delivering a complete response letter, the move may speak to “potential FDA bandwidth issues” and could bridge the gap to the U.S. launch in early 2027, according to the analysts, who noted that missed PDUFAs are rare and that the agency has had 11 months to review Savara’s data package.
The analysts also weighed the potential of manufacturing issues, as the FDA had previously refused to review a 2025 Molbreevi application due to chemistry, manufacturing and controls concerns. But Savara resolved those deficiencies and said in April that the three-month review delay wasn’t related to safety, efficacy or manufacturing issues.
Jefferies still holds “high confidence” in an approval for Savara’s asset, citing “compelling” Phase 3 data and long-term durability in an open-label extension. In the 48-week IMPALA-2 trial, Molbreevi significantly improved a measure of pulmonary function at 24 weeks compared to placebo, hitting the trial’s main endpoint. The drug candidate touts FDA fast track, breakthrough therapy and orphan drug designations.

Lose the Superbird: The Road Runner Hemi RTS Show Car Is the Wildest Winged Mopar of 1970
87 photos
Photo: Mecum
What's the most famous Mopar three-letter acronym of them all? GTX? GTS? TRX? AAR? SRT? ACR? R/T? HEMI? The last two aren't three letters by themselves, but their average is right on the money. But how about RTS? I’ll give you a moment to remember that body style, the platform, and powertrains. No, it’s a trick hint, there was no Chrysler Motors Corporation automobile named “RTS.” There were five of them, all Plymouths, all from 1970.
Standing for Rapid Transit System, it was Plymouth's loud, tire-roasting 1970 marketing blitz, cooked up specifically to match Dodge's beloved Scat Pack of 1968 and turn respectable family showrooms into high-octane sanctuaries for horsepower-obsessed youth.
Far from being just a catchy slogan slapped onto glossy brochures, the Rapid Transit System was an entire performance ecosystem. Plymouth urged dealers to build dedicated Rapid Transit System Centers stocked with High Impact colors, beefy drivetrains, aggressive axle gears, and race-bred parts forged in NASCAR, Trans-Am, and NHRA battles. Its purpose was bluntly simple: convince restless kids that Plymouth wasn't just grandma's Valiant store, and move serious iron fast.
The campaign ran through the 1970 and 1971 model years, landing at the glorious peak of Detroit's horsepower mania right before insurance actuaries dropped an anvil on the party. Five street-bruising production models anchored the official RTS lineup: the Road Runner, GTX, 'Cuda, Duster 340, and full-size Sport Fury GT, while the winged 1970 Road Runner Superbird loomed nearby like a hyperactive cartoon bird that accidentally swallowed an Acme rocket.
Photo: Mecum Truth be told, the Superbird was the only production vehicle that was styled just right for the Rapid Transit System , although that was a pure coincidence. Ma’ Mopar never intended to use the ‘Bird as a sales honeycomb for buyers. However, the preposterously in-your-face looks of the NASCAR-homologation muscle car served that purpose in full, planted in showrooms to catch the eye of passers-by, and lure them in the webs of a shrewd salesman that would convince them into a new car.
Because regular showroom muscle cars apparently looked too polite for 1970, Plymouth also launched the Rapid Transit System Caravan, a traveling road show hauled to dealerships, racetracks, and auto shows nationwide. Former Hot Wheels designer Harry Bradley sketched wild custom interpretations of Plymouth's lineup, birthing four one-off showstoppers across 1970 and 1971: a 1970 'Cuda 440, a 1970 Duster 340, a restyled 1971 Road Runner, and the magnificent headliner standing before us.
Meet the one-of-a-kind 1970 Plymouth Hemi Road Runner built specifically for the Rapid Transit System Caravan. While fabricator Byron Grenfell massaged the Duster and Chuck Miller's Styline Customs built the 'Cuda and later 1971 Road Runner, Plymouth entrusted this B-body bruiser to Roman's Chariot Shop in Cleveland, Ohio.
Photo: Mecum Showing just 1,700 miles on the odometer today, it spent far more time snapping necks under spotlights than dodging potholes on American highways, or slaying rivals at stoplights. After all, its looks alone could subdue any potential contender into second thoughts.
Subtlety took a sabbatical sick day hike and went AWOL when this coupe rolled into the paint booth. Roman's Chariot Shop drenched the body in candy gold beneath a pearl white roof, contrasting the glare with a flat black hood and flat black decklid. Lest anyone mistake it for a quiet commuter, oversized Road Runner birds were painted straight into the bodywork, practically daring Wile E. Coyote to drop an crate of dynamite at his own paws.
The custom bodywork went far beyond loud paint, as the shop reworked the sheet metal like kids handed unlimited clay and a welding torch. Enlarged air scoops give the flanks a hungry, “inhale-the-zip-code” attitude, while a molded rear spoiler finishes the tail.
Photo: Mecum (Sidenote: I don’t know who copied who on that rear deck lid element: Plymouth from Chrysler, or vice-versa? The Chrysler 300 Hurst from that same year had a strikingly similar wing, but far more subtle and discrete. The Road Runner RTS was about as low-profile as a one-bore punt gun blast at a puritans’ wedding ceremony).
The rear wheel wells were enlarged and flared out 4 inches over Ansen Sprint wheels, and shaved door handles leave the sides smoother than a used-car salesman's alibi. Up front, Plymouth's factory face entered the witness protection program. In its place sits a plastic honeycomb grille flanked by 9-inch square Cibie headlights, giving the Road Runner an intense glare that made stock 1970 B-bodies look half asleep.
Walk around back and a custom one-piece tail lens stretches cleanly across the tail panel, handing anyone left behind at a stoplight a full-width crimson receipt for their bruised ego.
Photo: Mecum Best of all, this wasn't some hollow fiberglass parade float pushed onto a turntable by nervous teen interns. Lift that flat black hood and you're staring straight at Chrysler's mythic 426-cubic-inch Hemi V8, factory-rated at a famously introvert 425 hp. Paired with a bulletproof TorqueFlite automatic transmission and a stump-pulling 4.10 rear axle, this elephant-powered Plymouth had the mechanical violence to back up every loud inch of its wild custom suit .
Pop those shaved doors and the cabin stays refreshingly focused while the exterior throws a disco party. Bucket seats straddle a center console, giving the driver a proper perch for wrangling 490 lb-ft of crank twist without sliding into the passenger's lap. Provenance hounds get spoiled silly here, too, with an official letter from the Chrysler-Plymouth News Bureau and the original, one-of-a-kind Rapid Transit floor runners crafted for both sides of the vehicle.
Surviving the 1970s intact as a factory show car was roughly as easy as smuggling a rhino in rut past TSA, and this gold Hemi vanished once its tour ended. For 20 years, Mopar fans feared the crusher had won. Then, in 1991, noted sleuths Steve Juliano and Ed Meyer tracked the missing bird down in Kalamazoo, Michigan, rescuing Plymouth's wildest rolling billboard before rust or bad taste could finish the job.
Photo: Mecum Even with a featherweight 1,700 miles showing, decades out of the spotlight meant the custom bruiser needed expert revival. In 2000, Ken Heckett restored the Road Runner to period-perfect glory, honoring every flare, scoop, and painted wing.
With its 1970 Caravan 'Cuda sibling having hammered for $2.2 million in 2023, the four surviving Rapid Transit System show cars now occupy Mopar's penthouse suite alongside the rarest winged warriors Plymouth ever built.
In 2019, at the Mecum Indy event, the 1970 Plymouth Hemi Road Runner Rapid Transit hammered 310,000 legal money of the United States of Automobile ($341k with the mandatory buyer’s fees). Before that, in November of 2018, it made a star appearance at the MCACN show – see the video embedded below, courtesy of Lou Costabile, the vlogger who’s always one snapshot away from musle car royalty .
Photo: Mecum It currently stands as the second-most expensive Road Runner ever (excluding the Superbirds and Richard Petty’s 1971 championship-winning car). Now, after decades turning heads in elite collections, this unmistakable slice of factory-sanctioned 1970 madness is strutting back under the auction spotlights.
Complete with its 426 Hemi thunder , Roman's Chariot Shop metalwork, News Bureau letter, and original dual floor runners, the one-off 1970 Plymouth Hemi Road Runner Rapid Transit System Caravan show car is offered for sale at the Mecum Kissimmee 2027 auction. Care to make a guess (educated of enthusiastic) on the high bid?

The new Renault Twingo E-Tech is among the most affordable vehicles, electric or gas-powered, starting at just £14,745 in the UK, or under $20,000.
Renault Twingo E-Tech prices and specs
Another affordable, practical EV the US will never see. Renault’s new Twingo E-Tech is an electric remake of its iconic 1990s city car.
The retro-looking EV went on sale in Europe earlier this year, starting at under €20,000 ($22,000), before government incentives. In places like Germany, it starts at about €13,990 ($15,500), including the €6,000 ($6,600) federal EV grant.
In the UK, Renault announced that prices for the Twingo E-Tech will start at just £14,745, or about $19,500. That includes the government’s Electric Clean Car Grant (ECG) of £3,750 ($4,900).
Advertisement - scroll for more content
At that price, Renault’s new electric car is among the most affordable vehicles available, including gas-powered cars.
It’s cheaper than the gas-powered Dacia Sandero (£14,765) and BYD’s cheapest EV , the Dolphin Surf (£18,675). Only a few cars are lower-priced, including the Dacia Spring (£11,990) and Leapmotor T03 (£12,995).
What do you get for the price? At just 3,790 mm (149.2″) long, the electric city car is a bit smaller than the Hyundai Inster and the BYD Dolphin Surf.
Renault Twingo E-Tech (Source: Renault)
For those in the US, that’s even smaller than the first-generation Chevy Bolt EV, which measured 4,145 mm (163.2″) in length.
Despite its compact size, the “cheeky, practical” 5-door city car, as Renault calls it, offers up to 360 liters of boot capacity. It also features independent, sliding 50/50 folding rear seats to haul bigger items like a surfboard.
With up to 50 kW DC fast charging, Renault said the Twingo E-Tech can charge from 15% to 80% in 28 minutes.
Renault Twingo E-Tech interior UK-spec (Source: Renault)
The base Renault Twingo E-Tech Evolution, priced from £14,745 ($19,500), uses a 27.5 kWh LFP battery and an 80 hp (60 kW) motor, delivering up to 163 miles of WLTP range.
The entry-level version features 16″ steel wheels, a 7″ driver display, 10″ navigation screen, and ADAS features, including cruise control and lane-keep assist.
Renault will offer three Twingo E-Tech trims in total. The mid-range Techno trim gains 18″ wheels, Google built-in with Renault’s Reno avatar, a reversing camera, automatic climate control, a hands-free key card, One Pedal driving, and heated front seats. It starts at £16,245 ($21,500), including the £3,750 ($4,900) ECG.
Renault Twingo E-Tech (Source: Renault)
With Google built in, drivers can easily find and navigate to charging stations via Google Maps, use Google Gemini AI virtual assistance, or access over 100 apps, including Waze and Amazon Music.
The top-spec Twingo E-Tech Launch Edition, priced from £17,645 ($23,200), including the £3,750 ($4,900) ECG, adds a suite of ADAS features, including blind-spot warning, rear cross-traffic alert and hands-free parking.
Inside, the Launch Edition features a special mottled textile upholstery with red stitching and premium floor mats.
Renault is offering a special promo for those who buy a new Twingo E-Tech through Mobilize Financial Services on a PCP or HP agreement by June 30, 2027, which includes two years’ free servicing.
Interested buyers can purchase the Twingo R Pass for £100, giving them priority access to ordering, a mini Twingo E-Tech model, and a green Renault key cover.
